name: Gareth Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the orthopaedic ward at the hospital in our market town, so broken hips, knee replacements, people who've come off motorbikes. It's a heavy ward, lots of hoisting, turning and getting people up on frames the day after surgery. I do pain relief, wound checks, pressure areas, and a lot of encouraging people who'd rather stay in bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's practical, it suits me after years in a warehouse. I trained late, at twenty-five, after the warehouse brought in picking robots. What wears me out is that I'm still learning the clinical side, and I lean on the senior nurse, Kofi, for anything with the drug charts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me, honestly. I've seen enough machines arrive in one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that hospitals should spend the money on beds and nurses, not on managers and consultants selling software. At work I'd say it straight. I don't post much, but I might share something on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a mixed bag. I left the warehouse because the robots were coming. If AI stalls now, I'll have swapped a dying job for a hard one that pays about the same. I'm in a room in a shared house, still paying off the loan I took to live while I studied, and I've got about two weeks spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and ask Kofi to sign me off on the drug competencies by summer. I'd put every bit of overtime towards the loan, which has about two thousand left on it. And I'd keep using the AI app now and then to revise, since a mate showed me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. The job's fine, the bank balance isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever regret leaving the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days, when my back's sore from the hoist and I check my pay. But the warehouse halved its pickers in two years. I'd rather be skint in a job that's still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if the loan was paid off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put that same money into savings every month, so I've got three months behind me. Then maybe a car that doesn't need a jump start every frosty morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds familiar. That's how the warehouse went, only slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office side that'll feel it, and the hospital should cut its own admin before touching the wards. At work I'd tell people to learn the new stuff once it's proven. I'd say to my mates that hard graft still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it changes my paperwork more than my hands. The care plans, the discharge letters and the ordering would go to the computer. I watched robots take over the warehouse aisle by aisle. They started with the paperwork there as well, and nobody noticed until the pickers went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system the ward brings in, once Kofi and the others had it running. I'd do weekend shifts with my uncle's removals firm for extra cash. And I'd keep paying down the loan, so I'm free of it before anything bigger happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've seen this film before and I know how it starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody noticed until the pickers went. What would the first sign be on the ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer ward clerks, and a new manager talking about efficiency. Then they'd stop replacing nurses who leave. That's what I'd watch for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want help from the government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts, no. I'd want proper apprenticeships, paid training on the job, like I wish I'd had. I paid my own way and I'd want others to be able to as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's the warehouse all over again, but faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people selling this should be held responsible for what it does to workers, and the hospital shouldn't throw money at it blind. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get a specialism quick. I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking work, charts and plans and ordering, is gone by 2028. Then the hands-on part, which is most of my job, lasts until about 2031. The orthopaedic ward is lifting, turning and hoisting all day. I give the robots until 2031 before they can do that, and I'm the junior who gets let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight for a specialist course, plaster room or theatre recovery, something skilled with my hands and my judgement. I'd take every removals weekend my uncle offers and save the lot. And I'd learn the AI tools on the ward early this time, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know what it's like to watch a job disappear, and I didn't enjoy it the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You usually wait for things to be proven. Why move early here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last time I waited, and by the time it was proven there were thirty of us going for three jobs. Two years doesn't give you time to watch. I'd move on the first sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine and I've got a plan. She worried enough when I left the warehouse. I'd tell her the truth once the plan was working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like how it should be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to train people properly on the job, and the hospital should run apprenticeships for new roles. At work I'd say learn it when it's proven, but don't hang about. I'd keep away from the arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-two when AGI comes and thirty-five when robots arrive. That's time to get good and specialise. In the warehouse I waited too long. On the ward I'll move when the first robot proves it works, not after the second one has my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my competencies, then go for the theatre recovery course in year two or three. I'd pay off the loan in the first year and then start saving. And I'd learn the ward's new tools once the first wards have them working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. It feels fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why theatre recovery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's skilled, it's hands-on, and it's people at their most vulnerable, just waking up. You need someone who notices a change in breathing straight away. I think that lasts longer than lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should help people through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help with training, yes, apprenticeships and the like. Not paying people to sit at home. Work's good for people, I've seen what happens to blokes without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare with ten years. I'd tell the lads at the pub to learn a trade that needs judgement. I'd be calm about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'll put it simply. Ten years is enough to do it the right way: learn the trade properly, pay off what I owe, and pick a corner of nursing that needs a person. I'd be thirty-seven and forty when it comes, and I'd want to be skilled by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, get experienced on the orthopaedic ward, and clear the loan. I'd use the AI tools once they're standard, like everyone else. And I'd save properly, aiming for three months behind me within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, because money's tight now. But I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your plans sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the hospital stop replacing nurses who leave. That's the sign I missed in the warehouse. I'd move the same month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Senior on a ward, or in theatre recovery. A small flat of my own, not a room. Not rich, but not counting every pound.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I've already lost one job to machines and that would be two in ten years. What would help is paid apprenticeships into the specialist roles, like theatre recovery, and the hospital cutting management waste before nurses. Nobody gave me anything for leaving the warehouse. I paid my own way into nursing, and I'd do it again if I had to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who've already changed careers once. We're the ones who know what it costs. Starting over at twenty-five was hard enough; at thirty-two it'd be harder.

headlineQuote: Nobody gave me anything for leaving the warehouse. I paid my own way into nursing, and I'd do it again if I had to.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a heavy **orthopaedic ward** who left a warehouse when robots came.
He rents a room, owes about **two thousand** on a study loan, and has two weeks spare.
He favours **apprenticeships** over handouts and blames waste and **managers**.
He's **uneasy** in most pictures and **anxious** at two years, remembering the warehouse.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would mean losing a second job to machines.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** into specialist roles and cutting **management waste** first.
